SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.
Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.
You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.
Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.
The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.
SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy , pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.
So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.
"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description .
The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit .
The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.
Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.
There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.
So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page .
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. articles.title_orig: Russia loses almost half a million lives in war on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russia loses almost half a million lives in war on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Death records reveal losses since full-scale invasion that are unprecedented in Russia’s modern history
Postwar ‘security guarantees’ a key focus in upcoming Abu Dhabi talks, says Rubio
More than 400,000 Russians have been killed fighting in Ukraine since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion nearly five years ago, according to data leaked from the state statistics agency, Rosstat.
The information, obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacking collective Silent Crow, contains more than 11m death certificates, including details of the deceased’s age, place of residence and location of death.
It was later shared with the Guardian and a small group of other media outlets.
According to the data, 412,576 death certificates explicitly linked the fatalities to the war, either through official cause-of-death codes or written references to combat and military operations.
The figures underscore the staggering human toll of Russia’s war against Ukraine, with no end in sight despite a fresh round of peace talks scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi this week.
The two hacking groups announced the breach on 1 November and published the data over the weekend. Rosstat confirmed it had been hacked but denied that any sensitive information had been obtained.
The dataset offers an unprecedentedly detailed picture of Russia’s wartime losses, which Moscow has sought to conceal. The Russian authorities have not published a death toll since the early months of the invasion, and information about military casualties is treated as a state secret.
The Guardian could not independently verify the authenticity of the entire dataset. However, the figures are broadly consistent with other estimates of Russian losses. British intelligence in September estimated that about 500,000 Russian soldiers had been killed since the start of the invasion.
Separately, the independent Russian outlet Mediazona has identified by name nearly 286,000 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine, drawing on official records, social media obituaries and photographs of gravestones. The outlet estimates the true toll is closer to half a million.
“The data looks authentic, and it’s very rich,” said Janis Kluge, the head of the Russia and Eurasia division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs.
“This is the biggest leak of data when it comes to Russian casualties,” added Kluge, who has studied Russian war statistics extensively.
The dataset is likely to underestimate the true death toll. Some soldiers remain missing, while others have never been identified.
Kluge also pointed to a significant delay between deaths occurring and being entered into official records, which he said typically took about six months.
“We are probably at this time closer to 500,000 killed Russian soldiers than 400,000,” he said.
The figures also reveal the unequal burden of the war across Russia, with poorer and more remote regions sustaining disproportionately heavy losses.
In Buryatia, Tuva and Zabaykalsky Krai, three regions in eastern Russia, war-related fatalities accounted for about a third of all deaths among men aged 18 to 49 between the start of the invasion and mid-2024. In Moscow and St Petersburg, the equivalent figure was about 10%.
There was also a sharp rise in Russian battlefield deaths as the war dragged on, with some of the deadliest months coming in late 2024 and 2025.
Kluge, who has been analysing the data, said the number of soldiers killed in several months during that period exceeded 15,000, equivalent to roughly 500 a day.
after newsletter promotion
“In late 2024 and in 2025, you see that the numbers in many months are above 15,000 per month, and that’s higher than I think most estimates were,” Kluge said. “That’s 500 a day, above 500 a day. Certainly shocking.”
The scale of the losses is staggering by any measure and unprecedented in Russia’s modern history.
In less than five years, Russian military deaths in Ukraine are estimated to have exceeded the combined death toll from all Soviet and Russian wars between the end of the second world war and the start of the full-scale invasion more than eightfold. The figure also exceeds the number of US military personnel who died during the second world war.
Rather than push Moscow towards a settlement, the scale of the losses is likely to harden Vladimir Putin’s resolve, according to a person familiar with the Russian president’s thinking.
“Putin understands these numbers, and for him to now settle for anything less than everything he wants would feel like a betrayal of himself and the people,” the person said.
Senior Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for the first US-brokered peace talks between them in nine months.
Previous negotiations have made little progress towards ending the war, with Moscow demanding that Ukraine withdraw from the parts of the Donbas region it still controls.
Neither Putin nor his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, will attend the talks. Instead, both countries will send senior delegations, with Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also expected to take part.
In a post on X, Witkoff said the negotiations would focus on “post-war security arrangement, de-escalation” and humanitarian issues.
European governments have expressed concern that the talks could extend beyond Ukraine to broader questions of European security, including Moscow’s longstanding demands for a reduction of Nato’s military presence in countries bordering Russia.
France’s foreign minister said Paris would participate in the negotiations but the Kremlin subsequently denied that France would be represented.

articles.title_orig: Zelda Ocarina's ReDead Were Set To Be "Very, Very Scary" In The Remake, But Nintendo Decided To "Dial It Back"
articles.title_zh: Zelda Ocarina's ReDead Were Set To Be "Very, Very Scary" In The Remake, But Nintendo Decided To "Dial It Back"
articles.content_orig:
Ocarina of Time's Switch 2 remake isn't really a scary game, but there are still some enemies throughout this adventure that may give players a fright.
Perhaps the most notable are ReDead , the zombie-like creatures that are difficult to escape when they set their sights on Link. These return in the remake and apparently were even scarier at one point during development, until Nintendo decided to "dial it back".
Here's what producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi had to say about this during a recent interview with GameSpot :
"With this remake, the graphics are a lot improved, and so the ReDead–the sound, the graphics, and the movement–ended up being very, very scary. And the staff wanted to make this in service of making a good gameplay experience. But from our perspective, taking a step back, we felt like, let’s remember the experience that we don’t want to change, and taking that into consideration, maybe we’ve gone a step too far, so let’s dial it back."
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
So, the decision was made to ensure the experience was more in line with the original game. The final result is the ReDead are still somewhat scary, but not "very, very scary" to the point it changes the experience.

articles.title_orig: Federal Reserve to Forgo Rate Decision at October 2027 Meeting
articles.title_zh: Federal Reserve to Forgo Rate Decision at October 2027 Meeting
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve won't vote on a potential interest-rate change at its October 2027 meeting, a departure that is part of a broader initiative from Chairman Kevin Warsh aimed at reducing the central bank's market footprint.
According to an announcement Thursday, the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will set aside its Oct. 26-27 session for "the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues."
Warsh announced the move at his news conference after the FOMC met in October, though he did not specify which meeting would be affected.
In 2027, there will be seven voting meetings, with the October session set up as extra time for policy deliberation without a formal vote or post-meeting statement. The new calendar shows that the final meeting of the year will now take place in November. It had previously been set for December.
"Now, what's the reasoning behind this change? To me, it's quite straightforward," the chairman said in explaining his rationale. "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals."
"But it's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations—for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point," he said.
Warsh has been critical of the Fed's prior communications strategy, saying policymakers spent too much time providing guidance on policy moves that handcuffed them when it came time to make decisions.
Under typical practice, the Fed meets eight times a year, following with a vote on interest rates and then a news conference from the chair.
Since Warsh took over, the post-meeting statement has been shortened dramatically. Moreover, the press question-and-answer sessions have been cut to around half an hour from their customary 45 minutes or so.
Warsh said in October that the meeting schedule is another step in his plan to streamline communication. He indicated last month that the number of nonvoting meetings would increase to two in 2028.
"I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail," he said. "It's an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions. It's yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track."
The FOMC next meets Dec. 8-9. Its first meeting in 2027 will happen Jan. 26-27.
Correction: The Fed's October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates. The headline in an earlier version misstated the year.

articles.title_orig: China stages unannounced Pacific drills in 'silent intimidation' of Taiwan, officials say
articles.title_zh: China stages unannounced Pacific drills in 'silent intimidation' of Taiwan, officials say
articles.content_orig:
The People’s Republic of China (PRC) may be conducting a major, unannounced military exercise that simulates surrounding and isolating Taiwan. The PRC likely aims to demonstrate that it can cut Taiwan off from air and sea during a conflict, eroding Taiwanese confidence in its ability to resist PRC aggression. Taiwanese National Security Council (NSC) Secretary-General Joseph Wu reported on November 3 that over 100 People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) and China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels were operating in the West Pacific.[1] Joseph Wu released data that appeared to show two main PLAN and CCG concentrations located between Taiwan and its principal partners, simulating isolation operations. The first concentration consists of four task forces from three different People’s Liberation Army (PLA) theater commands operating between Taiwan and Guam, including the Liaoning carrier strike group. ISW-CDOT reported that the strike group moved to the West Pacific via the Basilan Strait in the Philippines between October 23 and 26.[2] The second concentration includes at least six CCG vessels and an unspecified number of PLAN vessels surrounding Taiwan.[3] Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense (MND) detected 49 air sorties around Taiwan on November 2, an unusually high number that included 36 sorties south of Taiwan that may have flown to support the four task forces operating in the West Pacific.[4] Satellite imagery from November 2 detected the PLAN’s most advanced aircraft carrier Fujian leaving its base in Sanya, Hainan, due east, possibly toward southern Taiwan.[5] Satellite imagery of Sanya Naval Base suggests that at least three other major surface combatants left the base between October 26 and November 2. These deployments represent a significant portion of the PLAN’s combat power, including two of its three carriers and at least four of its ten guided-missile cruisers.[6]
The scale of these deployments suggests that the PLA is conducting a major exercise that simulates isolating Taiwan. The number of vessels involved and the geographic range of their deployment are greater than the PLA’s most recent exercise around Taiwan — Justice Mission 2025.[7] The coordination of surface forces from the Eastern, Northern, and Southern Theater Commands is rare. Major PLA exercises targeting Taiwan since 2022 have largely centered around the PLA’s Eastern Theater Command, the organization primarily responsible for Taiwan-focused operations.[8] The presence of four major surface groups beyond the first island chain from three separate theater commands could represent an effort to coordinate the principal surface combatants of all three coastal theater commands in a single far-seas operation. The positioning of major PLAN combatants in the West Pacific, between Guam and Taiwan, and combined PLAN and CCG forces conducting a closer encirclement of Taiwan also follow patterns from previous PLA exercises. Strait Thunder 2025a, for instance, involved an “inner” encirclement of Taiwan alongside a carrier strike group operating between Taiwan and Guam.[9] The recent PLAN maneuvers could improve the PLA’s ability to effectively deter or prevent outside forces from reaching Taiwan during a contingency by preparing its coastal theater commands to coordinate their forces during such an operation.
The PRC’s decision to not announce a major exercise departs from recent precedent and may aim to create the impression that the PLA can isolate Taiwan at will. The PRC normally announces and names major military exercises targeted against Taiwan and has done so for the last four such exercises.[10] The PRC has yet to announce a major military exercise at the time of writing despite the scale of the movements observed in the West Pacific. The PRC may seek to represent the presence of its forces surrounding Taiwan and in the West Pacific as routine, rather than exceptional. The PRC may also aim to demonstrate an ability to rapidly transition from a peacetime posture to combat operations, decreasing the time adversaries have to detect PLA preparations for a blockade or invasion of Taiwan. ISW-CDOT has assessed that the PRC aims to erode Taiwanese confidence in its own defense and in US willingness to come to its aid.[11] The PLA’s recent movements around Taiwan and throughout the West Pacific likely serve the dual purpose of preparing for a real isolation campaign while aiming to create informational effects that erode Taiwan’s confidence in its own defense and the ability of its allies and partners to support it.
The PRC dismissed Taiwanese claims of PRC interference in Taiwanese local elections as “political maneuvering” by the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) to bolster anti-PRC sentiment, even as Taiwanese authorities investigate nine cases of suspected foreign interference ahead of the vote. Taiwan’s National Police Agency stated at a November 4 press conference that it is cracking down on electoral disinformation and investigating nine cases of foreign interference, four of which have received indictments.[12] Taiwanese President William Lai Ching-te warned on November 4 that online disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks seeking to influence public opinion and disrupt access to campaign websites would increase ahead of the November 28 local elections.[13] ISW-CDOT previously assessed that the PRC appears to be attempting to influence the Taipei mayoral election, with the Taiwanese National Security Bureau (NSB) announcing that planned and sustained cyberattacks suspected of being conducted by the PRC are targeting DPP candidate Puma Shen.[14] The NSB assesses that the PRC has been significantly increasing cyberattacks against Taiwan in recent years.[15] Taiwan experienced an average of 2.63 million cyberattacks a day in 2025, more than double the amount reported in 2023.[16] The National Police Agency is likely investigating PRC interference based on these circumstances, though Taiwanese sources did not explicitly name the foreign actors involved. PRC Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) spokesperson Zhu Fenglian stated that Taiwanese claims of PRC “cognitive warfare” and “election interference” are fabricated to deceive voters and incite hostility against the PRC.[17]
Taiwanese drone developer AerosoarX and Ukrainian unmanned systems company UFORCE signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on November 4 to explore potential supply chain cooperation, expanding Taiwanese-Ukrainian private-sector defense cooperation and allowing Taiwan to test its emerging defense technology on Ukrainian battlefields.[18] AerosoarX and UFORCE hope to employ Taiwanese technology and manufacturing capacity to diversify UFORCE’s component suppliers, particularly through access to Taiwan’s semiconductor, electronic component, communications, and precision manufacturing industries.[19] AerosoarX founder Max Lo stated that the company has supplied drone subsystems and components to the US artificial intelligence (AI) company Rajant for US military projects and aims to begin producing its 15-inch AI-enabled, first-person-view drone in November 2026.[20] UFORCE produces unmanned maritime, land, and aerial systems in addition to AI software and command-and-control systems.[21] AerosoarX previously signed strategic cooperation memorandums with Rajant and US communications company SiMa.ai to cooperate on developing AI-enabled drones in October 2026.[22]
This cooperation stands to de-risk Ukrainian critical defense technology supply chains, which remain reliant on the PRC despite the PRC limiting exports of batteries and magnets used for drone motors to Ukraine.[23] Commercial Taiwanese-Ukrainian exchanges are essential for defense cooperation and increasing Taiwanese civilian preparedness. Ukraine is unlikely to establish formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan to avoid disrupting its relationship with the PRC, making commercial relationships essential for increasing Taiwanese-Ukrainian engagement.[24] Severa

articles.title_orig: BTC news: Prices slip below $70K, triggering $1.2 billion in liquidations
articles.title_zh: BTC news: Prices slip below $70K, triggering $1.2 billion in liquidations
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Bitcoin price fell below $69,000 for the first time since mid-August, as five separate pressures landed in the same week. The drop has pushed Bitcoin (BTC) onto its 200-week average, the line that anchored its summer recovery.
No single trigger explains the speed of the move. Leverage did, and a weekly close below the average could expose BTC holders to a much deeper retest.
Hotter-than-expected October inflation data has flipped the rate debate firmly toward tightening.
Traders now see no chance of the Federal Reserve (Fed) holding or cutting rates in December, according to CME FedWatch data.
Fed funds futures assign an 88.7% probability to a 25 basis point hike at the December 9 meeting. That would lift the target range from 3.75%–4% to 4%–4.25%.
The remaining 11.3% points to a larger 50 basis point move, taking the range to 4.25%–4.5%.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller has also said he would back a 25 basis point increase at the December meeting.
Historically, Bitcoin has struggled when borrowing costs climb, since tighter money pulls capital toward safer yields.
MSCI will remove Strategy, the largest corporate Bitcoin holder, from its benchmark indexes on November 30.
The exclusion does not force Strategy to sell any BTC. However, the MSCI exclusion rules could make raising fresh capital harder.
Strategy funds its BTC buying through those capital raises. Weaker access to investors could therefore slow one of the market's most consistent sources of demand.
US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) have shed $1.44 billion over five straight sessions, according to Farside Investors data.
The streak began on November 5, when $430.2 million left the funds. Another $411.9 million followed the next day.
BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) drove most of the selling. The largest spot Bitcoin fund accounted for roughly $1.07 billion of the five-day outflow.
Across all funds, November 4 is the only session with net inflows since the start of the month.
Not every product is losing money, however. Morgan Stanley's spot Bitcoin fund (MSBT), the cheapest on the table at a 0.14% fee, has drawn inflows in each of the last four sessions.
Early data for November 12 shows a further $47.7 million in outflows, with figures for IBIT and Fidelity's FBTC still pending.
ETF flows remain the clearest gauge of institutional appetite. Redemptions concentrated in the largest fund suggest big allocators are cutting exposure rather than buying the dip.
The sell-off forced $1.65 billion in liquidations over 24 hours, according to CoinGlass data.
Roughly 89% of those positions were longs. In other words, traders betting on higher prices were forced to sell into the decline.
Each forced sale pushed the price lower, which in turn triggered the next wave of liquidations.
Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the November 3 midterms, taking over in January 2027.
That puts the Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act, which would define how US regulators oversee crypto, in limbo. The bill already fell 49–50 in September's Senate cloture vote.
If it stalls through year-end, it effectively starts over under Democrats. House Democrats are already discussing a stricter alternative.
Still, any bill needs 60 Senate votes and Trump's signature. The bigger near-term cost is time, as regulatory clarity may slip into 2027 or later.
BTC is now testing its 200-week simple moving average (SMA) near $67,975. The average tracks nearly four years of closes and serves as a gauge of Bitcoin's long-term trend.
That same line caught BTC during the July sell-off and launched the August rally. A weekly close above it would keep the long-term uptrend intact.
If it gives way, the $66,000 to $67,000 zone is the next major support. That band capped every recovery attempt from June through August, and broken resistance often flips into support on a retest.
Below that, $62,300 stands as the final floor. Buyers stepped in there in late February and again before the late-August breakout.
A brief break under that level in July produced the $58,000 low.
On the upside, $75,000 is the first hurdle if BTC bounces. The level held as support through September and October before breaking this week.
Two dates will likely set the near-term path. MSCI's exclusion takes effect November 30, and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announces its decision on December 9.
A softer-than-expected Fed could revive a rebound toward $75,000. In contrast, a hike paired with continued ETF outflows would raise the odds of a test of $62,300.
The broader test is whether Bitcoin trades as a rate-sensitive risk asset or a long-horizon store of value. A weekly close below the 200-week average would point to the former.

articles.title_orig: Fed faces tougher inflation fight as pressure builds for more rate hikes
articles.title_zh: Fed faces tougher inflation fight as pressure builds for more rate hikes
articles.content_orig:
At the start of the year, the Federal Reserve was sanguine about the American economy. Inflation seemed to be trending down. The shock from President Donald Trump's tariffs was abating. Economists projected the central bank could lower rates .
Instead, the Fed was forced to raise rates in September for the first time since 2023, hiking 25 basis points as inflation, which has run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years , reemerged as its bugbear.
As the Federal Open Market Committee's final meeting looms on Dec. 8, October's consumer price index was higher than expected : 0.4% month-on-month versus the 0.3% predicted in a Dow Jones survey of economists. So-called core CPI increased 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast.
Now, traders are certain the Fed will raise rates next month, according to the CME Fedwatch tool . The only question is by how much. Almost 88% of traders expect another 25-basis-point hike. The rest expect a half-point hike.
The cost of living has been a top issue on Americans' minds. Vice President JD Vance cited it as a reason the Republican Party lost so much ground in the midterm elections.
"We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said in an interview with "PBS NewsHour " on Tuesday, adding that prices are "on everyone's mind" and calling inflation readings "borderline disturbing."
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said Tuesday that a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, adding this should be on the table if core CPI were "around 0.3%."
"The latest CPI print strengthens the near-term case for tightening, even though a 25 basis point hike should be sufficient for December," Chester Liaw, G7 Economist at OCBC Group Research, said on Thursday.
Even with a hike, inflationary impulses could remain, Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at PGIM, said in a note Thursday.
With the Democrats in control of Congress next year, Trump could use executive actions to increase tariffs, Sockin said.
Since the labor market remains stable, Sockin said, he doesn't expect rising interest rates this year to derail "significant portions" of the U.S. economy, leaving open the door to future increases.
"We continue to expect the Fed to hike rates by 100 bps with the next increase coming in December and quarterly thereafter," Sockin added.

articles.title_orig: The downfall of Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: The downfall of Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
The US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between a Chinese businesswoman who had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing.
There is disagreement among US officials about the strength of the evidence that Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Chinese equivalent of the CIA, to spy on Jensen Huang — and, by extension, on US policymakers.
The FBI has been investigating Huang’s affair for at least a year. But Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that there are still “no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me, or by [FBI] Director Patel around who she is or is not.” President Donald Trump also hedged Thursday on whether the US had determined she was a spy, when commentator Stephen A. Smith asked whether Huang was right to have stepped down as CEO.
“Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” Trump said. “But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.”
Some officials at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, including those close to director Jay Clayton, have framed the characterization of Alice Huang as a Chinese spy as not entirely accurate and over-torqued, sources said. And officials at the CIA also are not yet convinced that the intelligence collection on Huang to date, including intercepted communications, proves she was knowingly funneling information back to Beijing, a source told CNN.
Still, some Trump officials told CNN that it strains credulity to believe that she was not acting as an agent of the Chinese government — simply by virtue of the fact that she is a successful Chinese businesswoman working with one of America’s most powerful companies .
Under Chinese national security law, Chinese citizens can be compelled to help gather intelligence on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party. Even if she had not done so yet, given her access to Huang — and by extension, to  Trump — some officials believe she posed a clear counterintelligence risk. But to others, the fixation on Huang’s relationship to the Chinese government has obscured broader questions around the US government’s failure to crack down on the diversion to China of sophisticated technology vital to the AI race.
Alice Huang’s Singapore-based company Megaspeed is a major purchaser of NVIDIA chips. The Department of Justice and the Commerce Department began an investigation into the firm in 2024 — part of a broader probe into an ecosystem of foreign shell companies suspected of diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China, a person briefed on the investigation said.
There are now questions brewing inside the White House over why the Commerce Department did not put Megaspeed on the so-called “entity list,” which restricts trade with companies that may pose a risk to US national security or foreign policy interests — at least while the investigation was ongoing, according to a person familiar.
“An intelligence operation wasn’t necessary to achieve that result,” a former Commerce Department official told CNN, noting that Jensen Huang has publicly advocated for the US to sell more chips to China. The fact that chips might be diverted to China through Megaspeed was, theoretically, a place where China’s interest already coincided with Nvidia’s — and “a regulatory loophole” already allowed it, the former Commerce official added.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Wednesday, following days of reports that he had had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Reports also emerged on Wednesday night that he separately had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia.
Democratic Rep. Jim Himes, the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, told POLITICO Thursday that he left a classified briefing with senior intelligence officials earlier this week unsure of the nature of Huang’s relationship with the Chinese government.
“What’s the relationship with Alice Huang and the Chinese, and what do we know about what influence or information was traded? Because today, at least, I don’t know,” Himes said.
Last year, when US intelligence officials first learned of the relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, officials across the government immediately wanted to know more — and some began sounding the alarm.
Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio warned in a memo in the spring about Jensen’s relationship with Huang, one source told CNN. But it is unclear how detailed the memo got on how much information Huang was or was not sharing with the Chinese government. Rubio briefed Trump on Jensen Huang and his relationship with Alice Huang aboard Air Force One en route to China in May.
The briefing occurred before Jensen Huang joined Trump in Alaska for the final leg of the trip, a source briefed on the matter told CNN.
Different agencies have continued conducting their own reviews of the intelligence, sources said. One particularly alarming development occurred when US intelligence  obtained communications that appeared to indicate someone with close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia was the source of information that ended up in Chinese intelligence streams, a person familiar with the investigation told CNN.
The FBI, which is conducting the primary counterintelligence investigation, told lawmakers last year that it was particularly suspicious of Alice Huang’s seemingly overnight career pivot from Chinese State television journalist to businesswoman with an unusually large amount of purchasing power in the Chinese economy, one of the sources said.
That, paired with her close relationship to the then-Nvidia CEO has continued to raise red flags inside the bureau, where the counterintelligence probe remains ongoing, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
Definitively linking suspicious behavior by Chinese nationals interacting with the United States to a state-directed spying campaign remains a perennial problem for counterintelligence officials trying to defend against Chinese espionage. It is notoriously difficult to collect intelligence on China, and China routinely compels its private citizens to do its bidding overseas.
When it comes to Chinese spying, the threat is in the eye of the beholder — some officials think the fears are overblown, other officials see a Chinese spy in every encounter.
“A lot of these people are guilty of just being Chinese,” said a former senior counterintelligence official.
But Joshua Hodges, a commissioner on the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, which investigates how US-China trade and economic ties affect American national security, said that “we’ve seen repeatedly the Chinese are incredibly adept at using people both wittingly and unwittingly.”
“Ultimately, what we typically see is those people, at a certain point in time, recognize that they know who they’re working for and they know the ends that they’re working towards,” he told CNN.
Hodges, who served on the National Security Council in Trump’s first term, noted Huang’s past rhetoric denouncing the phrase “China hawks” as “a badge of shame.”
“That clearly is directed to make people stop talking about the topic,” Hodges said. “You’ve got the biggest, one of the biggest, CEOs in the world attacking people for speaking out about something they care about — that clearly only benefits one country.”
CNN’s Kristen Holmes and Alejandra Jaramillo contributed to this report.

articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
Russian President Vladimir Putin and members of the Russian delegation outlined Russia’s steadfast commitment to its original territorial demands of Ukraine and ultimatums to dismantle NATO and the post-Cold War European security architecture following the latest trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on November 12. Putin remains unwilling to compromise on any of these demands. Putin met with US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and Former Senior Advisor to the US President Jared Kushner on November 12 in Moscow City following the November 10-11 US-Ukrainian-Russian peace talks in Abu Dhabi.[1] Several Russian officials have publicly commented on the negotiations and made various suggestions in recent days about ending the war, but statements from Putin and members of the current Russian negotiating team represent the official Russian negotiating position and clearly demonstrate that the Kremlin remains unwilling to compromise on its original war demands.[2]
Putin is refusing to accept any proposed future demilitarized zone in post-war Ukraine or to abandon his demand that Ukraine hand over the parts of Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts that Russian forces have not seized. Putin stated at his meeting with Witkoff and Kushner that Russia considers its state border (which Russian law defines as including the four illegally annexed oblasts) to be the only clear “demarcation line” between Russia and Ukraine.[3] Putin claimed that contested “gray zones” in Ukraine are unclear and that peace talks that discuss such gray zones will not lead to a lasting, stable peace. Putin’s statement implies that he will not accept a demilitarized zone in Ukraine and that he wants to be able to deploy Russian forces along a potential new post-war Russian-Ukrainian border. Putin is also indicating that he will only accept a peace settlement that grants Russia full control over all of Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts. Russia enshrined its illegal annexation of these four regions into its constitution in 2022, and 2020 constitutional amendments prohibited actions to alienate any part of Russia’s territory.[4] Russian officials, including Putin, have repeatedly declared that Moscow considers the entirety of the four annexed regions to be part of the Russian Federation even though Russian forces do not fully occupy those regions.[5] Putin’s November 12 statement is consistent with his June 2024 speech to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA), in which he called for Ukraine’s withdrawal from the entirety of the four illegally annexed regions, even parts that Russian forces did not — and still do not — occupy.[6] Kremlin officials often cite Putin’s 2024 speech as Russia’s non-negotiable position to end the war.[7]
Putin is also unwilling to cede the territory in northern Ukraine that the Kremlin claims Russian forces have seized but that lies outside of the four illegally annexed oblasts. Putin’s November 12 statement about the state border as a “demarcation line,” coupled with recent statements from members of the Russian negotiating team, demonstrates that Moscow intends to retain its control over areas of northern Ukraine that it considers a necessary “security zone.”[8] Vladimir Medinsky, a Russian presidential aide and head of the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi, stated on November 11 that Russia will not accept any territorial exchanges with Ukraine and will continue to expand its “security zone” in Ukraine (referring to territory in northern Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts).[9] Medinsky and Putin have also publicly stated that any territory on which a Russian soldier sets foot belongs to Russia.[10] The full extent of the areas in Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts that Moscow aims to claim remains unclear.
Putin continues to reject all meaningful Western security guarantees for post-war Ukraine. Putin reiterated on November 12 his demands that Western states refrain from deploying troops to Ukraine as part of any post-war security guarantees.[11] Putin stated that the presence of any foreign troops on Ukrainian territory is “absolutely unacceptable” for Russia and would threaten Russian security. Putin reiterated claims that foreign troops would be “legitimate targets” for Russian forces and that their deployment to Ukraine would immediately restart the war.[12] Putin and other Russian officials have rejected Western security guarantees for Ukraine since the European-led Coalition of the Willing began discussing such foreign deployments in March 2025.[13]
Russian negotiators used the Abu Dhabi talks to reassert their 2021 demands of NATO. An informed source told Ukrainian outlet RBC Ukraine on November 11 that Russian negotiators in Abu Dhabi refused to discuss meaningful ceasefires or concessions with Ukraine and insisted on focusing talks on the Kremlin’s December 2021 demands to halt NATO’s eastward expansion; give Russia a veto over military deployments to countries that joined NATO after 1997; refrain from military activity in Ukraine, Eastern Europe, the Caucasus, and Central Asia; and refrain from deploying intermediate-range missiles within range of Russian territory.[14] The 2021 ultimatums also demanded that the United States commit to upholding the ban on NATO enlargement and refrain from deploying weapons in Europe. Two sources familiar with the matter told Axios on November 11, however, that Kushner and Witkoff told Russian negotiators that the situation in the world has changed significantly since 2021 and that Russia should draft a new peace proposal that would lay out Russian steps to de-escalate and ensure Russia does not renew aggression against Ukraine and Europe.[15] Russian negotiators’ continued insistence on Putin’s 2021 demands directly contradicts Witkoff and Kushner’s reported position and demonstrates that the Kremlin has no interest in serious negotiations to end its war in Ukraine. Russian negotiators reportedly also falsely claimed that Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 because former US President Joe Biden failed to respond to Putin’s December 2021 ultimatum.[16] US officials, in fact, repeatedly tried to negotiate a de-escalation of tensions between Russia and Ukraine in late 2021 and early 2022. Biden, for example, held a videoconference with Putin in December 2021, and then-US Assistant Secretary of State Wendy Sherman met with Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov in January 2022 in an attempt to de-escalate tensions arising from Russia’s military buildup on the Ukrainian border.[17]
Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022 to subdue and subsume Ukraine as part of a larger Kremlin project to restore the Russian Empire and to destroy NATO as a meaningful alliance, as ISW has repeatedly assessed.[18] Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022 because he assessed that the war could achieve both of these goals, not because he perceived a threat from NATO. Putin’s December 2021 ultimatum to NATO, which remains the foundation of Russian demands to Europe, serves this same purpose, and the Kremlin’s continued commitment to the December 2021 demands shows that Moscow has no interest in any meaningful compromise or negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
Putin is simultaneously doubling down in his efforts to convince US officials to accept Russia’s fictitious frontline. Putin reiterated his false July 3 claim that Russian forces have full control over Kostyantynivka, Donetsk Oblast, in his meeting with Witkoff and Kushner and proposed that Russia and Ukraine could conduct a humanitarian mission in Kostyantynivka as a continuation of recent humanitarian work in occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast.[19] Putin proposed inviting international media representatives and Ukrainian and Russian human rights representatives to oversee the evacuation of civilians from Kostyantynivka and to show who actually controls the town. articles.title_orig: Is Nvidia Undervalued?
articles.title_zh: Is Nvidia Undervalued?
articles.content_orig:
It's been a brutal few weeks for Nvidia ( NVDA -4.34% ) investors. After reaching an all-time high of roughly $243 per share in early October, the artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker has experienced an epic sell-off.
On Nov. 12, Nvidia stock crashed as low as $148.80 following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang. Huang's departure follows revelations concerning two extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's board of directors has been investigating the allegations, which have not established that Huang compromised company secrets.
Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress is now serving as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent replacement. The uncertainty has rattled investors. However, the resulting sell-off has created an interesting valuation opportunity.
Nvidia stock is trading at one of its cheapest valuations in more than a decade. Here's why I think the recent decline could represent a compelling buy-the-dip opportunity.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/12/26
One useful valuation metric for evaluating a growth stock is the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio . This tool compares a company's current share price with analysts' expectations for its earnings over the next 12 months. Simply put, a lower ratio means investors are paying less for each dollar of anticipated profits.
As of this writing (Nov. 12), Nvidia's forward P/E hovers around 11, according to data from Yahoo! Finance. This is the lowest reading dating back to May 2016, according to data compiled by TradingView.
For perspective, Nvidia traded near 90 times forward earnings in late 2021. Nvidia has become a much larger and more profitable business since then, and yet investors are now assigning it a fraction of its former earnings multiple.
Of course, a lower multiple does not necessarily mean a stock is undervalued . If Nvidia's future earnings disappoint, today's seemingly attractive valuation could prove misleading. Nevertheless, the historical comparison suggests investors are pricing in considerable uncertainty about the company's future.
Despite Nvidia's cratering stock price, its latest financial results show little evidence of deteriorating demand. During its fiscal second quarter of 2027, Nvidia generated $96.2 billion in revenue, representing a 106% increase year over year. The data center business contributed $89 billion, growing 117% annually. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings per share surged 120% to $2.22.
These results reflect the enormous spending on AI infrastructure from Microsoft , Amazon , Alphabet , Meta Platforms , Oracle , Anthropic, and OpenAI. Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs are central to many hyperscale projects, while its new Vera Rubin architecture is entering production. The company is also expanding into Vera CPUs, high-speed networking equipment, and specialized AI inference accelerators.
Importantly, Nvidia expects its momentum to continue. Management's guidance for the fiscal third quarter calls for $108 billion in revenue, plus or minus 2%. That would represent roughly 89% growth compared with the same quarter last year.
Nvidia is scheduled to report those results on Nov. 17 . If the company delivers another strong quarter and maintains an encouraging outlook, investors may begin reassessing whether its valuation profile accurately reflects its growth trajectory.
There's an important distinction between an undervalued stock and a risk-free investment. Huang was instrumental in developing Nvidia's technology roadmap, forging customer relationships, and building its competitive advantages.
Competitors such as Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom are working to capture more AI infrastructure spending. Furthermore, many of Nvidia's largest customers are developing custom silicon , potentially reducing their dependence on the company's GPUs over time.
Nevertheless, Nvidia's moat isn't going to crack just because of a leadership transition. The company's CUDA software ecosystem, advanced chip designs, networking technology, and customer relationships help form strong barriers to competition.
At roughly 11 times forward earnings, I think Nvidia's recent decline has created a unique opportunity for long-term investors. To me, Nvidia offers an unusually compelling combination of growth and valuation.
While Nvidia stock will almost certainly experience additional volatility as investors assess the company's next CEO, investors willing to tolerate that uncertainty by investing in Nvidia at a substantial discount to its historical valuation could witness lucrative gains as AI infrastructure build-outs continue accelerating.

Sviyazhsk (Buyan-M) (Project 21631) class corvette Grad (575), commissioned in 29 Dec 2022, one year before sister-ship Naro-Fominsk (595). Naro-Fominsk was reportedly struck by Ukraine in the Gulf of Finland on 11 November 2026. (Michael Nitz)
The Finnish Defence Forces ( Puolustusvoimat : FDF) detected a strike against a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland on 11 November 2026 and has monitored developments since, an FDF spokesperson told Janes on 12 November.
There is no immediate military threat to Finland, and the security situation in the Baltic Sea remains stable, the FDF spokesperson said. The FDF would not disclose further details about the incident's location or timing, or how it was detected and identified.
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said it had planned and carried out an attack on the Project 21631 Buyan-M-class small missile corvette Naro-Fominsk . The SBU did not specify the weapon used or provide evidence of damage caused to the vessel.
The SBU linked the attack to a wider operation against port, oil-processing, and transport infrastructure at nearby Ust-Luga near St Petersburg on the night of 11 November. The Armed Forces of Ukraine said five oil-product tanks, with a combined capacity of 150,000 m 2 , were damaged, and a large fire broke out.
The Buyan-M can carry Kalibr cruise missiles and P-800 Oniks anti-ship missiles, the SBU said. Russian forces have used both missile types in attacks on Ukraine.
Commissioned on 23 December 2023 and assigned to Russia's Baltic Fleet, Naro-Fominsk is 74.1 m long, has a beam of 11 m, and displaces 949 tonnes. It has a top speed of 25 kt and is armed with a 100 mm A-190 gun.

articles.title_orig: Four grizzly bears killed Canadian mother and daughter, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Four grizzly bears killed Canadian mother and daughter, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
Canadian wildlife officials say DNA testing linked an adult female grizzly and her three offspring to the deaths of a mother and daughter near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Investigators say the attack likely involved predatory behavior.
Four grizzly bears have been linked through DNA evidence to a deadly attack on a mother and daughter in British Columbia , prompting Canadian wildlife officers to kill all four animals, officials announced Tuesday.
The British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said forensic testing conclusively linked an adult female grizzly and her three offspring to the deaths of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, near Bella Coola.
The bears were captured over the weekend and killed in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety, according to a Nov. 10 statement from the agency.
BODY OF MISSING HIKER DISCOVERED OFF TRAIL AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE RARE DEADLY BEAR ENCOUNTER
An image showing a photo of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, who were killed in a grizzly bear attack. (Facebook/Josh Kara Balcarras)
Investigators determined that the encounter likely involved predatory behavior, although officials did not elaborate on how the attack unfolded.
"This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," said Insp. Jeff Tyre in a news briefing.
More than a dozen conservation officers participated in the response, helping recover the victims, collect evidence and locate the bears while working in difficult terrain and weather conditions.
GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL
FILE – Grizzly bear in Jasper National Park, Canada. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
Balcarras, an art therapist, and Reed went missing after taking a walk on the Snooka West Trail near their home.
Family members contacted the Royal Canadian Mounted Police after Balcarras missed a scheduled online meet-up. Investigators found her vehicle at the trailhead before recovering her body on Nov. 2 and Reed's body on Nov. 3.
The agency said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a separate 2025 grizzly bear attack on a school group near Bella Coola that injured 11 people, including students and teachers.
The investigation has concluded, although officials said further analysis will examine the response and circumstances surrounding the attack.
Royal Canadian Mounted Police board, on April 10, 2024, in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The conservation service said fatal grizzly bear attacks involving predatory behavior are rare and encouraged people traveling in bear country to leash pets, travel in groups and learn how to reduce the risk of wildlife encounters. Fox News Digital's Louis Casiano contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
Published 13 November 2026 7:17am
Share this with family and friends
Environmental activist Greta Thunberg has slammed Australia's track record on climate action at COP31 talks in Türkiye, saying "even a snail would agree" that the country needs to move faster.
The 23-year-old's appearance alongside speakers from Australia, Nepal, Rwanda and Gaza caused traffic chaos inside the United Nations' climate summit in Antalya on Thursday, which also heard criticism of Australia's ongoing mining approvals.
Australia's Energy Minister Chris Bowen will lead negotiations at the annual event, which has drawn more than 92,000 attendees, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrived on Wednesday for the leaders' summit portion of the event.
Asked whether she agreed with comments about Australia's slow record on climate action, Thunberg said her opinion was obvious.
"Even a snail would agree with that," she told the crowd.
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"It's common sense. It doesn't get more clear than that."
Thunberg previously spoke at the event in 2018 and 2019 but criticised the COP26 event in 2021, describing it as "blah, blah, blah".
She returned this year to bring attention to the state of the climate, she said, and call for action to prevent further disasters.
"We are all here because we know that the climate crisis is already here and now, and it is already a matter of life and death," Thunberg said.
"And these disastrous trends we are seeing unfold all over the world are going to continue to exponentially get worse and worse.
"We have to start acting accordingly."
Indigenous woman Rikki Dank also spoke at the event, saying Albanese should listen to calls from Traditional Owners to stop approving new and extended fossil fuel projects.
"He needs to stop speaking and start listening to the Australian people when they say no more new coal, oil and gas," she said.
"He needs to stop speaking and start listening to our brothers and sisters across the world when they say they don't want us to export coal, oil or gas and the climate harms that they bring with them."
Albanese and Bowen have so far declined to address proposals to transition away from fossil fuels at the COP31 event, instead discussing electrification and renewable energy targets.

articles.title_orig: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.title_zh: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.content_orig:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife
T he vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster .
The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.
The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.
It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.
Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.
Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.
“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.
“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”
Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.
“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.
More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.
Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.
Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.
Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.
after newsletter promotion
Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta , two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.
Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.
Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.
According to a Wall Street Journal report , the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.
In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on 30 October that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining.
In Oman , divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands.
But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said.
Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.”
Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems.
A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar – the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down – on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea.
Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface.
“Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades – so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

articles.title_orig: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then see Zelenskyy in Dublin
articles.title_zh: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then see Zelenskyy in Dublin
articles.content_orig:
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow Thursday to discuss Ukraine, after two days of U.S.-led talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi yielded no major breakthroughs.
“I think progress was made. I think it was made earlier today,” Witkoff told reporters after the meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin. “People didn't think that we were going to restart trilateral. We’ve restarted it. We’ve set a new meeting. This is what President [Donald] Trump wants to see."
He went on to say that a European representative would be present for the next stage of the talks, which are set to look at the continent’s wider security arrangements. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he said.
Witkoff and Kushner are now en route to Dublin, where they are set to brief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on any developments from the talks. Zelensky is among the dozens of world leaders in the Irish capital for the European Political Community summit.
Zelensky has expressed optimism about the next round of negotiations, saying there is a "window of opportunity” to reach a peace deal with Russia.
“There really is this window of opportunity, when all the participants involved in this negotiating process could get the result by the beginning of 2027,” he said , speaking alongside Irish Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Micheál Martin during a press conference in Dublin.
Although Russian and Ukrainian negotiators ⁠reported some progress during this week's Abu Dhabi talks—including a prisoner swap agreement—all sides have acknowledged that significant differences remain, particularly over territory.
Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin's demands to surrender the entirety of the eastern Donbas. With negotiations over territory deadlocked, U.S. mediators instead sought to steer discussions toward post-war security guarantees and reconstruction.
However, Putin doubled down on his opposition to the idea of foreign peace-keeping troops being stationed in Ukraine if an agreement is reached, telling Witkoff and Kushner it would be considered by Russia as a "continuation of war."
Fully integrating European representatives into future negotiations could also prove challenging, despite Witkoff's confidence on the matter. Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who led Russia's delegation in Abu Dhabi, previously expressed skepticism over any European involvement.
Yuri ⁠Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy adviser, ​ told reporters ⁠after the Moscow meeting that the Russian President will continue talks on Ukraine with Trump ‌at the Asian-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in ‌China later this month.
Despite the major obstacles that remain, Trump has expressed renewed optimism about ending the war—a goal he had previously claimed would be achieved on his first day back in office in 2025. “We're seeing a very strong inclination to end [the war between] Russia and Ukraine,” the President insisted during a press conference Monday.
The European Union is preparing a new sanctions package against Russia in an effort to increase economic pressure on Moscow and strengthen Ukraine's position in future peace talks.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, alongside a separate proposal to address Ukraine's financial needs, by the year-end.
“We are, as a Commission, preparing a proposal [on] how to cover the financial needs of Ukraine in 2027, we will come with the sanctions package and the proposal for the financial needs before the next European Council,” she told reporters in Dublin. “We will support Ukraine, be it at wartime, or be it at peacetime."
The next European Council meeting is scheduled to take place in Brussels across Nov. 26-27.
Other European leaders also took the opportunity to underscore the importance of bolstering Ukraine.
French President Emmanuel Macron said that “without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” insisting “there is no more U.S. support.”
In an address at the summit, Zelensky appealed to Europe to continue supporting Ukrainian territory and championed sanctions against Russia as an effective measure.
In a separate display of solidarity, the U.K. government announced new levies targeting Russia's 10 largest oil producers. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the move as “a sweep of stinging new sanctions to turn the screws on Russia’s oil revenues and drive forward an end to the Kremlin’s needless war.”
Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Antonio Costa, president of the European Council, stand alongside Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and French President Emmanuel Macron at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Nov. 12, 2026. Brian Lawless—Getty Images
As Witkoff and Kushner were meeting Russian officials in Moscow, Zelensky raised concerns about new speed restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade sister version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service.
Zelensky said the Ukrainian military was facing "systematic" restrictions to Starshield and, as a result, struggling to intercept Russian drones. "This is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," he said . "We are trying to clear up all circumstances with the American side."
TIME has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.
Starlink offers Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit. Its sister service Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon, relies on the Starlink network and has become a vital component for Ukrainian forces, strengthening its far-reaching drone strike missions and air defenses.
Last month, Ukraine complained that speed restrictions had been imposed on Starshield, leading to the “ failure ” of several military missions. There were conflicting reports as to how the service came to be restricted.
Reuters, citing three U.S. officials, had reported that the decision to limit the service came from inside the White House.
When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.”
When initially addressing the matter, SpaceX founder and CEO Musk emphasized how Starlink and Starshield are different. He cited the U.S. authorities as being in control of the latter’s usage determinations.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” he said on X. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
Musk later said his company SpaceX had imposed limits on the use of its Starlink satellite system, accusing Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity. He denied being behind the simultaneous issue with Starshield.
Kyiv denied breaching Starlink’s terms of service. “It’s very strange that Elon Musk doesn’t know about the restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine,” said Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov via Telegram . “Starlink does not work over Russian territory. So we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and mid-range strikes.”

The U.S. Air Force abruptly relocated more than a dozen aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England amid an emerging security threat, U.S. officials confirmed Tuesday.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the move, citing sources who said the threat originated in Iran.
As U.S. officials assessed the threat's nature and urgency, commanders raised the base's security level to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the military's second-highest alert level, indicating a likely terrorist threat against personnel or facilities.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
U.S. Air Force KC-135, used for in-flight refueling, takes off from RAF Mildenhall Airbase. (AP Photo/Max Nash, File)
Flight-tracking data and open-source analysts with the Military Air Tracking Alliance identified 13 U.S. aircraft leaving the base late Monday, the Associated Press said.
Nine Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers were moved to airfields in Scotland, Germany and Spain.
Three CV-22B Ospreys were relocated to nearby RAF Lakenheath, which has hardened aircraft shelters.
A U.S. official told The Associated Press the moves were precautionary, noting that some aircraft were on rotational deployments while others were permanently stationed in the United Kingdom .
IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY
American aircrews check a B-52 Stratofortress long-range subsonic bomber aircraft on the pan at RAF Fairford. The United Kingdom reportedly is refusing to let the United States use the base for a potential attack on Iran. (Getty Images)
The move marks the second major relocation of U.S. military aircraft from Britain in less than two months.
In early October, the Air Force pulled heavy bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after British counterterrorism police stopped three suspicious vans headed toward the base Sept. 27.
Two men have since been charged under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.
Separately, the Justice Department unsealed indictments against three Iranian-backed operatives on Tuesday accused of involvement in coordinated terrorist plots across Europe, including RAF Fairford.
UK POLICE ARREST 'EXPLOSIVE' SUSPECTS NEAR US AIRBASE, KEY TO IRAN WAR
The main gate of RAF Fairford is pictured on September 27, 2026 in Fairford, United Kingdom. (David Bown/Getty Images)
RAF Mildenhall is home to the 100th Air Refueling Wing, the only permanently based U.S. tanker wing in Europe.
Its KC-135 Stratotankers support allied aerial refueling and long-range strike missions across the region.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Washington routinely repositions military forces.
"We are constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons," Rubio told reporters when asked about the evacuation.

articles.title_orig: Home sales in worst slump since the aftermath of the Great Recession
articles.title_zh: Home sales in worst slump since the aftermath of the Great Recession
articles.content_orig:
Home sales fell to their lowest since 2010, a new report shows, in large part due to high mortgage rates. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.
Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.
"It was a punch in the gut," said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com . "We expected to see a soft month but not the softest month since 2010."
The drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.
In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023. Rates have gone down a bit since then, but are still well above where they were a year ago.
Higher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.
The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September to increase the cost of borrowing, including home mortgages. Fewer home sales and other purchases mean less economic activity, which the Fed wants in order to reach its goal of lowering inflation.
Policymakers at the Fed have signaled another rate hike could come in December, which could further slow down the housing market.
"It might seem like kicking the housing market while it's down right now for the Fed to continue a rate raising cycle but in the long run getting inflation under control is really the goal," Berner said.
